Main question: How do computers communicate over a network?

---
 Let's start with the question - What is a computer network? 
# What is a computer network?
> A computer network is a communications medium. That's all. Nothing more. A "computer" can be digital, analog, or organic in the form of people which is where the term "computer" was first applied, that is to "one who calculates". In that sense a "computer network" can be verbal, nonverbal, analog, digital... etc, etc.
> - b4xt3r from [a reddit post](https://www.reddit.com/r/InformationTechnology/comments/efqch1/serious_question_what_exactly_is_a_computer/)

I like this particular idea of a computer network because it's more generally accurate.

So the basic idea of a computer network is that it's a communication medium that allows two or more computers to exchange data.

Now let's say you wish to send a meme to your friend and a work-related report to your colleague form your computer, how do you/your computer know which computer belongs to your friend and should be sent the meme and which computer belongs to your colleague and should be sent the report? How does a computer know what, where, or who the other computer is? 

- How does a computer know exactly which computer to send the data to?

From what I know, IP address is used to uniquely identify devices over a network.


# IP Address
IP stands for Internet Protocol.

>An Internet Protocol address (IP address) is a numerical label, such as 192.168.1.1 or 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334, that is assigned to a device connected to a computer network that uses the Internet Protocol for communication.
> - [Wikipedia - IP Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IP_address)

- What is the Internet Protocol?
- Who assigns the IP address to a device?

## Internet Protocol

> The Internet Protocol (IP) is a protocol, or set of rules, for routing and addressing packets of data so that they can travel across networks and arrive at the correct destination. Data traversing the Internet is divided into smaller pieces, called packets. IP information is attached to each packet, and this information helps routers to send packets to the right place. Every device or domain that connects to the Internet is assigned an IP address, and as packets are directed to the IP address attached to them, data arrives where it is needed.
> - [Cloudflare - What is the Internet Protocol?](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/network-layer/internet-protocol/)

muscle-protein-metabolism-mpm.title: Muscle Protein Metabolism (MPM)
muscle-protein-metabolism-mpm.content:
Muscle protein synthesis (MPS) is the metabolic process where the body builds and/or repairs skeletal muscle proteins.
Muscle protein breakdown (MPB) is the opposite. It's the metabolic process of breaking down the muscle proteins.

##### Protein Turnover
The body is in a constant state of protein synthesis and protein degradation which is known as protein turnover. A continuous process of replacing the broken proteins by synthesising proteins.

Net balance = Protein synthesis - Protein breakdown

Muscle growth occurs when the net balance is positive i.e. MPS > MPB.

%%What causes muscle protein breakdown?%%

# Muscle Protein Synthesis
%%What causes muscle protein synthesis?%%
- resistance exercise and dietary protein intake
- **Resistance Exercise (Mechanical Tension):** Lifting heavy weights or training to failure creates mechanical stress and micro-tears in muscle fibers. This stimulates MPS for up to 24 to 48 hours post-workout.
- **Essential Amino Acids (EAAs) & Leucine:** Consuming protein provides the building blocks (amino acids) needed to construct new muscle. The specific amino acid **leucine** acts as a primary trigger that turns on the **mTORC1** pathway, instructing ribosomes to build new muscle proteins.
- Insulin: Released in response to meals, insulin helps suppress muscle protein breakdown (MPB), shifting the body into a positive net protein balance. 
- Adequate Recovery & Sleep: Deep sleep supports hormonal balance and optimal myofibrillar protein synthesis, whereas sleep deprivation impairs muscle recovery.

making-of-this-website-how-i-post-notes-.title: Making of this website - How I post notes directly from within Obsidian
making-of-this-website-how-i-post-notes-.content:
04.11.2026
16:59

After redoing this website many times over, I finally decided to go for a really simple blog-style website and then add more things later as and when needed.

Now this website just contains a few of my notes from Obsidian but the way I post, remove, and update those notes is the fun part. Since my Obsidian is full of notes that are incomplete, irrelevant, or personal, I needed a way to post the notes selectively. 

# The setup
- front-end-only
- made in React
- hosted on GitHub Pages

After working on the UI initially, I just vibe coded the rest once the website had a consistent theme. I ~~stole~~ took inspiration from [Cloudflare's website](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/) and replaced their orange with a light crimson.
## Fetching the data
Since the website is front-end-only and hosted on GitHub Pages I had to make the data accessible by either adding it directly to the website folder or uploading it on a public URL, allowing the website to fetch the data.

The original approach that I used was to dump all the data from notes I wanted to post into an `articles.json` file in the public folder of the website. Then fetch that file from the base URL.
```typescript
const res = await fetch(`${import.meta.env.BASE_URL}/articles.json`, {
	headers: { "Cache-Control": "no-cache" },
});
```

But since I am using gh-pages module to deploy the website to GitHub Pages, the `gh-pages` branch is used to build the website instead of `main`. I was only updating the `articles.json` file in the main branch, which means I had to execute `npm run deploy` every time I wanted the changes to reflect in the gh-pages branch thus consequently on the live website.

Rebuilding and redeploying the website for every note update is an overkill and waste of resources. I also considered updating the `article.json` file in both branches simultaneously but that would defeat the whole purpose of using git and branches. Or just pushing the changes directly to the gh-pages branch and then sync the main branch with it. But any push made to the branch being used by GitHub Pages redeploys the website automatically, which is, again, not necessary.

To address all those issues I changed to only updating the file in the main branch and fetching data from it directly through `https://raw.githubusercontent.com` instead of using base URL.
```typescript
const res = await fetch('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Arveix/archives/refs/heads/main/public/articles.json');
```

I dropped `cache: 'no-cache'` in the new request because it trigged CORS preflight check which sends an `OPTIONS` http request resulting in a `403 Forbidden` response from GitHub.

![[Screenshot 2026-11-04 at 4.26.15 PM.png]]

And apparently `raw.githubusercontent.com` forces a 5-minute cache from their end so setting cache options on client's side is pointless. I couldn't find any official source for it but the `200 OK` response headers do have `cache-control: max-age=300` attribute.

With this setup the website doesn't redeploy unnecessarily and the repos are maintained properly.

# The problem
Wanting to choose specific notes to post meant that I couldn't just automatically upload the entire Obsidian Vault folder periodically. I had to figure out a way to not only select specific notes but then continue tracking them in order to handle renamed or deleted notes and more importantly keeping Obsidian notes and the website blogs in sync by automatically updating the blogs as I edit the notes.

# The solution
The simplistic approach would have been to manually add or upload the specific notes that I wanted to post. But doing a repetitive task manually is just plain annoying and a little stupid. 

My first solution was to write a little shell script using which I could run a single command in the terminal with the name of the note/file passed to it as an argument. It would copy the file into a 'articles' folder inside my website folder. 
```bash
cp "/Users/arveix/Obsidian Vault/$1" "/Users/arveix/.../archives/articles/"
```

Sure, this made the task a little easier but that still meant that for every update I'd have to open the terminal, manually run a command and type the name of the file. After which I'd have to also push these changes to GitHub.

The idea that was floating around in my mind was a "Publish" button for individual notes, similar to what blogging websites or Wordpress have.
My requirements were:
- Easy way to publish notes from within Obsidian itself
- Should not have to manually type out file names at any point
- The blogs on website should automatically update when the associated note in Obsidian is updated

Basically, I wanted to continue using Obsidian as usual without disrupting my flow of taking notes by constantly worrying about updating the website.

I implemented this solution using two core parts:
- Using Obsidian properties to create a "publish" button
- A Python script that periodically checks the Obsidian Vault folder for changes (running as a daemon)

## The "publish" button
This is the ingenious part of the solution, the part that makes it exciting for me.
Obsidian properties contain the metadata and are stored as YAML frontmatter in the `.md` files.

![[Screenshot 2026-11-04 at 5.21.49 PM.png]]

![[Screenshot 2026-11-04 at 12.19.00 PM.png]]

The way I implemented the publish button is by using the tags. To publish a particular note, all I have to do is to add a "publish" tag in the Obsidian properties.

![[Screenshot 2026-11-04 at 12.23.26 PM.png]]

And then this little snipped of code does the trick:
```python
if 'publish' in (post.metadata.get('tags') or []):

publishDate = all_articles[slug]["publishDate"] if slug in all_articles else datetime.now().isoformat()

all_articles[slug] = {
"title": file_name.stem,
"tags": [tag for tag in post.metadata.get('tags', []) if tag != 'publish'],
"publishDate": publishDate,
"content": post.content
}

else:

all_articles.pop(slug, None)
```

Every time the python script checks for changes, this bit of code adds only the notes with a publish tag to the `all_articles` dictionary and the rest of the irrelevant notes are left as is. And the else statement removes any notes present in `all_articles` which no longer have a publish tag so removing the publish tag "unpublishes" a note.

I quite literally get a publish/unpublish button and never have to leave Obisidian to post/manage the notes on the website.

## The Python script
This python script is where all the actual work happens. 
Initially I wrote a script using the `watchdog` library that watches a given folder for any changes. The script would then update those changes into an `all_articles` dict and dump it into the `/public/articles.json` inside the website folder. That solution works nicely for live updates. On a local server, the notes on the websites would be updated instantly as I type/make changes in Obsidian.

However, there was no point in pushing live updates since the unmodifiable 5 min cache enforced by `raw.githubusercontent.com` limits website updates regardless of how fast the notes data is updated.

In the new implementation of the script, I entirely dropped the `watchdog` library. Instead the flow of the process is as follows:
1. **Check if Obsidian is active**
   I used an AppleScript via the `subprocess` library to returns which app is currently 'frontmost' (i.e., active).
   ```python
   def get_active_app():
    applescript = '''
    try
        tell application "System Events" to get name of first application process whose frontmost is true
    on error
        return ""
    end try
    '''
    try:
        res = subprocess.run(['osascript', '-e', applescript], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
        return res.stdout.strip()
    except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
        print(f"Error: {e.stderr.strip() if e.stderr else e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return None
   ```
   
2. **Conditions to update the notes**
  This Python script also tracks the time since last update (of the notes). The conditions to run the notes update function are:
  - Obsidian is active and time since last update > 300s
  - Obsidian was active and it not active anymore
  
  ```python
  while True:
    current_app = get_active_app()

    is_active = current_app.lower() == target.lower() if current_app else False

    if is_active and (time.time() - last_update > 300):
        print('Obsidian is active. Looking for file changes.')
        was_active = True

        file_timestamps = update_archives(file_timestamps)
        last_update = time.time()
        print('Last update: ', last_update)

    elif not is_active and was_active:
        file_timestamps = update_archives(file_timestamps)
        last_update = time.time()
        print('Last update: ', last_update)
        
        was_active = False
        print('Obsidian is now inactive.\n')
        
    time.sleep(1)
  ```
  
3. **Update function** 
  The update function is where the checking for change and pushing updates takes place.

  `all_articles` stores the data from `articles.json` file used by the website:
  ```python
  try:
    with open(articles_json_file_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
      all_articles = json.load(f)
    except (FileNotFoundError, json.JSONDecodeError):
      all_articles = {}
  ```
  
  Whereas `file_timestamps` variable holds the paths of `.md` files from Obsidian Vault and their 'last modified' timestamps:
  ```python
  file_timestamps = {f: f.stat().st_mtime for f in Path(FOLDER_PATH).rglob("*.md") if f.is_file()}
  ```

  `update_archives` function checks for changes in file_timestamps, updates the `article.json` accordingly and pushes the changes if there are any:
  ```python
  def update_archives(file_timestamps):
    file_timestamps, modified_files, deleted_files = get_modified_files(file_timestamps)

    if not modified_files and not deleted_files:
        print('No changes.')
        return file_timestamps

    for file_name in deleted_files:
        slug = generate_slug(file_name.stem)
        all_articles.pop(slug, None)

    for file_name in modified_files:
        post = frontmatter.load(file_name)

        slug = generate_slug(file_name.stem)
        
        if 'publish' in (post.metadata.get('tags') or []):
            publishDate = all_articles[slug]["publishDate"] if slug in all_articles else datetime.now().isoformat()

            all_articles[slug] = {
                "title": file_name.stem,
                "tags": [tag for tag in post.metadata.get('tags', []) if tag != 'publish'],
                "publishDate": publishDate,
                "content": post.content
            }
        else:
            all_articles.pop(slug, None)

    with open(articles_json_file_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            json.dump(all_articles, f, indent=4, ensure_ascii=False)
    
    subprocess.run(["git", "-C", GIT_REPO_DIR, "add", TARGET_FILE], check=True)
    status_check = subprocess.run(["git", "-C", GIT_REPO_DIR, "status", "--porcelain", TARGET_FILE], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    
    if status_check.stdout.strip():
        subprocess.run(["git", "-C", GIT_REPO_DIR, "commit", "-m", "Auto commit: updated articles"], check=True)
        subprocess.run(["git", "-C", GIT_REPO_DIR, "push"], check=True)
        print('Updated articles.json')

    return file_timestamps
  ```
   
This whole process keeps repeating every five minutes and that's how the blogs on this website are automatically updated whenever I make changes to a published note in Obsidian.

## Running the script as a daemon
The final step was to always keep this script running in the background so I used `launchd` to run this script as a user agent by creating a `com.user.updatearchives.plist` config file in `~/Library/LaunchAgents` folder:
```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://apple.com">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>Label</key>
    <string>com.user.updatearchives</string>

    <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array>
        <string>/Users/arveix/scripts/.venv/bin/python3</string>
        <string>-X</string>
        <string>utf8</string>
        <string>-u</string>
        <string>/Users/arveix/scripts/update_archives.py</string>
    </array>

    <key>EnvironmentVariables</key>
    <dict>
        <key>LANG</key>
        <string>en_US.UTF-8</string>
        <key>LC_ALL</key>
        <string>en_US.UTF-8</string>
    </dict>

    <key>RunAtLoad</key>
    <true/>

    <key>KeepAlive</key>
    <true/>

    <key>StandardOutPath</key>
    <string>/tmp/updatearchives.out.log</string>
    <key>StandardErrorPath</key>
    <string>/tmp/updatearchives.err.log</string>
</dict>
</plist>
```

By default, launchd uses the macOS version of Python if you pass only `python` or `python3` as an argument. That gave me an error because the `watchdog` library needed python 3.10+ version. You can provide the absolute path to the Python binary you want to use, even if it is located inside a virtual environment: 
```xml
<string>/Users/arveix/scripts/.venv/bin/python3</string>
```

I also had to move the script out of Desktop since it's a protected folder.

The script's standard output and standard error streams are stored in specific files based on this section of code:
```xml
<key>StandardOutPath</key>
<string>/tmp/updatearchives.out.log</string>
<key>StandardErrorPath</key>
<string>/tmp/updatearchives.err.log</string>
```
However these streams are buffered by default, only printing the output in batches.

Adding the `-u` flag makes these output streams unbuffered, allowing you to see the logs in real time:
```xml
<array>
    <string>/Users/arveix/scripts/.venv/bin/python3</string>
    <string>-X</string>
    <string>utf8</string>
    <string>-u</string>
	<string>/Users/arveix/scripts/update_archives.py</string>
</array>
```

Now the script keeps running in the background at all times and updates the website automatically.
![[Screenshot 2026-11-04 at 8.19.16 PM.png]]
It uses 11.0 MB of RAM and about 0.5% of the CPU based on the Activity Monitor.


# Future Scope
Next step for me would be to set up auto-sync for Obsidian notes across all of my devices and modify this Python script to run on other operating systems too since this version is specific to macOS.
